nameStory: The 'great skua' gets its name from the Faroese word 'skúgvur,' reflecting its northern Atlantic origins. In Britain, it's often called a 'bonxie,' a delightfully quirky name that comes from the Shetland Islands where these robust seabirds are well-known for their aggressive behavior around nesting colonies.
description: The Great Skua is a powerful, gull-sized seabird that's built like the bully of the beach. About the size of a Herring Gull but much stockier and more muscular-looking, it has dark brown plumage with lighter streaking and a thick, hooked bill perfect for its piratical lifestyle. These maritime marauders make their living by catching fish at the ocean surface or, more dramatically, by chasing other seabirds until they drop or regurgitate their catch.

idTips.label: Stocky Build
idTips.description: Much more robust and barrel-chested than a typical gull, with broad shoulders and a thick neck that gives it a powerful, almost hawk-like silhouette in flight

idTips.label: Dark Plumage
idTips.description: Overall dark brown coloring with golden or buff streaking on the head and neck, lacking the clean whites and grays of most gulls

idTips.label: White Wing Patches
idTips.description: Distinctive white patches at the base of the primary feathers create bold white 'windows' visible in flight, flashing like beacons against the dark wings

idTips.label: Heavy Bill
idTips.description: Thick, dark, hooked bill that looks more raptor-like than gull-like, perfectly designed for tearing flesh and intimidating other birds

idTips.label: Aggressive Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen harassing other seabirds in spectacular aerial chases, diving and swooping until the victim drops its fish

habitat: In New England waters, Great Skuas are extremely rare visitors to offshore waters, typically seen far from shore during migration or winter wandering. They prefer deep ocean waters where they can find the concentrations of seabirds they rely on for kleptoparasitism (stealing food). When spotted, it's usually from whale-watching boats or during organized pelagic birding trips many miles offshore.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring records exist of birds potentially moving north toward Arctic breeding grounds, most likely spotted in April or May during pelagic trips.
seasonality.summer: Virtually never seen in summer as breeding adults remain in the far North Atlantic around colonies in Iceland, Scotland, and Norway.
seasonality.fall: The most likely season for New England sightings, when post-breeding birds or juveniles may wander south along the Atlantic, though still exceptionally rare.
seasonality.winter: Occasional winter records exist of birds found in deep offshore waters, following concentrations of wintering seabirds they can harass for food.

funFact: Great Skuas are such effective aerial pirates that they've earned the nickname 'sea hawks' – they can force a gannet diving from 100 feet up to regurgitate a fish in mid-air, then catch that fish before it hits the water, essentially getting restaurant-quality seafood delivered by personal butler!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with dark-phase jaegers, but Great Skuas are noticeably larger and bulkier with broader wings, lacking the pointed tail projections that jaegers often show. Remember: skuas are the 'bulldogs' of the seabird world – short, stocky, and built for intimidation.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'Great Skua,' this species is actually smaller than the South Polar Skua, which can also rarely appear in New England waters. The 'great' refers more to their fierce reputation and dominance over other seabirds rather than their absolute size.
compareHints: Great Skuas are much larger and more robust than their jaeger relatives (Parasitic, Pomarine, and Long-tailed Jaegers). Unlike jaegers, which are more elegant and falcon-like, Great Skuas have a bulldozer build with broader wings and lack the long tail streamers that adult jaegers often display. Think of jaegers as sports cars and Great Skuas as armored trucks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Parasitic Jaegers are intermediate in size between the smaller Long-tailed Jaeger and the bulkier Pomarine Jaeger.
Pomarine Jaegers are the bulkiest of the three regular jaeger species in New England waters, noticeably stockier than the slender Long-tailed Jaeger and chunkier than the Parasitic Jaeger.
Among the three jaeger species found in New England waters, the Long-tailed is the smallest and most delicate, with the most pronounced tail streamers when adult.
Unlike the smaller jaegers in its family, South Polar Skua has a much heavier build and shorter, squared tail rather than the elongated central tail feathers of adult jaegers.
